# RetailCast India — Approach Summary / Technical Decision Log

*(~1,490 words. Every number below is regenerated by `src/audit.py`; the model by `src/forecast.py`.)*

## Q1. Audit method (~155 words)

I audited provenance before performance, in six passes. **(1) Coverage/integrity:** day-range of every file — `sales` and `market_signal` stop at `d_1913` while `calendar`, `sell_prices` and `vendor_signal` reach the horizon — plus sales sanity (non-negative integers, continuous day index, no duplicate dates). **(2) Feed provenance:** for each vendor feed I correlated its value against actual `units` at lags −2…+2, checked behaviour on zero-sales days, and the value/units ratio — the test for whether a "signal" leads demand or is a disguised copy of the target. **(3) Vendor backtest** against trailing-mean baselines. **(4) Regime scan:** last-90-vs-prior-year level per series, plus first/last non-zero day for births/deaths, cross-checked against sibling series. **(5) Feature usefulness:** price/units correlation, festival uplift, weekday profile. **(6) Adversarial sweep:** duplicate/mirrored series, SNAP-flag signal, horizon-event coverage, month-of-year seasonality. I stopped when every feature had a number-backed keep/drop decision and no sweep check surfaced an unhandled effect.

## Q2. Data verdicts (~500 words)

**V1 — `market_signal.csv` is target leakage and unavailable at prediction time.**
*What:* all 60 series, `d_1`–`d_1913` only. *Evidence:* mean per-series `corr(units, mkt_signal)` = **0.92 at lag 0**, collapsing to **0.37 at lag ±1**; `mkt_signal` is **exactly 0 in 100%** of zero-sales rows and never 0 when `units>0`; the median value/units ratio is **~10** (so `mkt_signal ≈ units × 10 × ε`). It ends at `d_1913`, so it does not exist for `d_1914`–`d_1941`. *Action:* excluded entirely. *Rejected reading:* "a leading demand index worth forecasting forward." Ruled out because a genuine leading indicator peaks at a **positive** lag, not lag 0, and would not be identically zero exactly when sales are zero — that is contemporaneous target contamination, and there is nothing to join to on the horizon anyway.

**V2 — `vendor_signal.csv` is legitimate but too weak to trust as the forecast.**
*What:* all 60 series, `d_1`–`d_1941` (covers the horizon). *Evidence:* never exactly 0 on zero-sales days (mean 3.9), weak within-series day-to-day corr (**median 0.10**); on a last-28-day backtest its **per-series WAPE = 1.04 vs 0.82** for a plain trailing-28-day mean. *Action:* not used as the forecast; kept only as an optional inspection anchor. *Rejected reading:* "a vendor baseline is safe to submit or weight heavily." Ruled out by the backtest — a free trailing mean beats it per series, so leaning on it would import error.

**V3 — Store `KA_3` is in a real, store-wide demand decline (regime change).**
*What:* all six `KA_3` series, over roughly the **last 100 days (≈ d_1815–d_1913)**. *Evidence:* last-90-day mean is **0.25–0.49× the prior-year mean** for the five meaningful-volume series; the same product in other stores holds ~1.0 (e.g. `HOMECARE_1_DETERGENT`: KA_3 ratio **0.25** vs **0.69–1.90** elsewhere). *Action:* for `KA_3` the level uses a **28-day window** (vs 42) so the forecast sits on the current regime, not an average dragged up by prior years. *Rejected reading:* "random dip / noise in a few SKUs." Ruled out because the drop is coherent across **all six** products in the one store, i.e. a store-level cause (footfall/closure), not per-SKU sampling noise.

**V4 — `HOMECARE_2_AGARBATTI_MH_4` is a late introduction.**
*What:* first non-zero sale at `d_268` (`d_1`–`d_267` all zero), then normal intermittent sales; no series dies early. *Action:* the recent-window level ignores the pre-introduction zeros automatically. *Rejected reading:* "a dead/erroneous series to drop" — ruled out because it sells normally after introduction.

## Q3. What I left alone (~180 words)

I deliberately did **not** clip the festival spikes — e.g. `GROCERY_3_ATTA_MH_3` = **612 units on d_303 (Diwali, 2018-11-04)**, ~5× the series' positive-day median. A naive "winsorise the top 1%" would remove them, but they are genuine recurring festival demand (event days average **1.31×** non-event), and the horizon itself contains festivals — clipping real peaks would bias festival forecasts low. Restraint is safe here because the spikes are old (2018–2020), far from the horizon, and my level uses a 42-/28-day recent window. Two further checked-but-immaterial signals I left alone: the **SNAP flags** (`snap_MH/KA/TN`) show ~**1.00** demand lift — a US-dataset artifact with no signal here — so I engineered no SNAP feature; and **April seasonality** — pooled history shows April below my Feb–Mar level window for ATTA (**0.88**) and AGARBATTI (0.64), but the clean 2022 analog is milder (ATTA **0.95**) and a month-of-year adjustment was a wash on backtest, so I did not bake in a seasonal haircut I couldn't validate.

## Q4. Modelling choices (~245 words)

**Final model (per series):** `forecast = recent_level × day-of-week multiplier × festival uplift`, clipped at 0. Level = mean of the last 42 days (28 for `KA_3`); the DOW profile comes from the last 180 days (weekend lift is real: **Sat 15.7 vs Tue 9.3** pooled); festival days get **1.15×** (measured uplift ~1.3×, discounted to avoid over-fitting sparse events).

**How Q2 shaped it:** V1 → `market_signal` excluded; V2 → `vendor_signal` not used; V3 → the short, per-store-adaptive window is the mechanism that respects the KA_3 regime, so regime information enters through the *estimation window*, not a dummy; near-zero price elasticity (median corr **−0.03**) → price excluded.

**Considered and rejected:** (a) a pooled gradient-boosted model with lag/rolling features — rejected because it would ingest the leaked `market_signal` and the KA_3 break makes global lag features misleading; high overfitting risk against a noise-floored horizon. (b) Per-series ETS/ARIMA — reasonable, but with 14 highly intermittent series (>70% zeros) and short usable regime windows it adds fragility for no backtest gain. (c) Submitting `vendor_forecast` — rejected by V2's backtest. (d) A vendor blend — tested; it did not beat the recency model on any holdout, so it was dropped. The rubric's flat accuracy curve rewards a robust, honest baseline over a fragile "clever" one.

## Q5. Validation I trust (~205 words)

I used **three rolling 28-day holdouts**: train `≤ d_1829 / d_1857 / d_1885`, scoring the next 28 days each. I scored the competition metrics — mean **RMSSE** (per-series, scaled by the in-sample 1-step naive error) and volume-weighted **WAPE**. Results: RMSSE **0.891 / 0.819 / 0.829**, WAPE **0.506 / 0.398 / 0.366** (means ≈ **0.85 / 0.42**). The `d_1830–1857` window (Jan–Feb) is the hardest — post-festival normalisation — which is exactly why I kept three windows instead of quoting the rosier pair. I **expected horizon mean RMSSE ≈ 0.83–0.90**, WAPE ≈ 0.38–0.45.

Why honest: every backtest uses only data before its cut, so the leaked `market_signal` never enters. The clearest way local validation could flatter the horizon is season: all three holdouts fall in Jan–Apr, but the true horizon is **all-April — the one month I cannot backtest**, since it exists only in the horizon and in prior years. The pooled April/Feb-Mar ratio for ATTA is **0.88** (the 2022 analog alone is milder, **0.95**) — both below 1.0 — so my flat carry may over-forecast ATTA, the volume driver and main WAPE lever, by roughly **5–12%**. I widened the expected range for it and flag it in Q6 rather than hard-coding an unvalidated correction.

## Q6. Least-sure call (~155 words)

The `KA_3` treatment. I **hold** the recent (28-day) level flat across the horizon rather than extrapolating the observed decline. If the store is still sliding I over-forecast KA_3 again; if the decline has bottomed out, extrapolating down would over-correct. With one more day I'd fit a short local trend on the last ~60 KA_3 days and test, on the `d_1886–1913` holdout, whether a gentle downward slope beats a held level — a statistically clear negative slope that *continues* through the holdout would move me. I hedged by choosing the 28-day window (which already leans the level toward the current regime) but stopped short of projecting further decline, because over-extrapolating a trend into a 28-day horizon is the more common and damaging error. The April/ATTA seasonal call (Q5) is a close runner-up, resolved the same way — hedge, don't hard-code — because it is likewise unbacktestable.

## Q7. Reproduce and stress (~100 words)

```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt && python src/forecast.py --data data --out submission.csv
```

Would the pipeline catch a *new* problem of the same family next month? **Partly, and honestly not fully automatically.** The recency window self-heals a *new* regime shift (a different store declining) without code changes, because the level always tracks recent days. But it would **not** automatically flag a *new leaked feed*: `market_signal` is excluded by name, so a differently-named contaminated feed would need me to re-run `audit.py`'s lag-0 / zero-day test. So: regime changes — the pipeline; new leakage — me, via the audit. I'd wire the lag-0 correlation and zero-day checks into a pre-flight assertion to close that gap.
